content: Nurses, alongside other healthcare professionals, are responsible for the treatment, safety, and recovery of individuals who are acutely or chronically ill or injured. They also play a critical role in maintaining the health of well individuals and managing life-threatening emergencies across various healthcare settings. Additionally, nurses may engage in medical and nursing research and perform numerous non-clinical tasks essential to healthcare delivery. The education, regulation, roles, and titles of nurses differ across countries, reflecting varying levels of responsibility and professional status. Nurses are tasked with developing and implementing care plans in collaboration with patients, their families, and other healthcare professionals. They also coordinate care provided by other team members, such as physical therapists, physicians, social workers, and dietitians. Nurses frequently act as advocates for their patients. Globally, the nursing profession is structured into distinct levels based on education, responsibility, and skill. A key distinction exists between task-based nursing and professional nursing. Increasingly, nurses are employed in advanced practice roles, such as clinical nurse specialists and nurse practitioners, who are qualified to diagnose health conditions and prescribe treatments. At the highest level of nursing education, doctoral-prepared nurses may hold a PhD or other doctoral degrees, specializing in research, clinical practice, or education. These nurses contribute to advancing the science and art of nursing through practice, teaching, and research. The educational requirements for nurses vary significantly worldwide. For instance, in some parts of Eastern Europe, nurses may only need a high school diploma and 12 to 18 months of training, whereas in Chile, registered nurses must hold at least a bachelor's degree. In the United States, there are over two million registered nurses, making up approximately 13% of the healthcare workforce. While nursing remains a predominantly female profession, the number of male nurses is steadily increasing. For example, in the U.S., the percentage of male registered nurses rose from 2.4% in 1980 to 5.4% in 2000, representing a 226% increase over two decades. Healthcare settings involve a diverse range of professionals who collaborate with nurses. These include nursing assistants, orderlies, auxiliary nurses, and healthcare assistants, who work under the supervision of registered or licensed practical nurses. Their duties include providing basic care, taking vital signs, assisting with hygiene and feeding, and offering psychosocial support. Technicians, such as certified medication aides, phlebotomy technicians, and surgical technologists, also play specialized roles. Pharmacists dispense medications and provide expert advice on drug therapies. Allied health professionals, such as respiratory therapists, medical technologists, speech therapists, occupational therapists, and physical therapists, work closely with nurses in multidisciplinary teams. In Australia, registration as a registered nurse requires at least an associate degree, which serves as the foundation for further specialization. Postgraduate diplomas and master's degrees offer advanced training in specific areas, while professional doctorates are available for those pursuing the highest levels of expertise. Historically, post-basic courses in areas like midwifery, psychiatric nursing, and intensive care were offered, but these are now provided as postgraduate diplomas or certificates. Enrolled nurses receive training through the Technical and Further Education (TAFE) system, typically lasting 12 to 18 months, with some states allowing them to administer medications and perform injections. The practice of nursing is regulated by state and territorial authorities, with the Australian Nursing and Midwifery Council (ANMC) facilitating a national approach to regulation. Nurses in Australia are categorized as nurse practitioners, registered nurses, or enrolled nurses. The traditional titles of sister and matron are no longer commonly used, and most nurses prefer to be addressed by their first names. Nurse practitioners have been part of the Australian healthcare system since 2000, reflecting the recognition of their advanced clinical expertise in areas such as wound management. In Canada, most provinces require registered nurses to hold at least a bachelor's degree, preferably a Bachelor of Science in Nursing (BScN). However, Quebec allows graduates from CEGEP to become registered nurses. While many practicing nurses are college graduates, new entrants to the profession are encouraged to pursue university-level education. Canadian nurses are categorized as registered nurses (RNs), licensed practical nurses (LPNs) or licensed vocational nurses (LVNs), and registered psychiatric nurses (RPNs), the latter being licensed only in certain provinces and territories. The regulation of nursing in Canada is managed at the provincial and territorial levels, adhering to principles endorsed by the International Council of Nurses. In Ontario, both RNs and RPNs are regulated by the College of Nurses of Ontario, whereas in other provinces, RNs and LPNs are governed by separate bodies. In western provinces, psychiatric nurses are regulated under distinct legislation. In Alberta, registered nurses and nurse practitioners must maintain clinical competence to receive an annual practice permit from the College and Association of Registered Nurses of Alberta, which also sets standards for scope of practice and provides professional support.
